records.description: Architectural gazetteer of Glamorgan in the Buildings of Wales series (the Pevsner series), first published in 1995 by Penguin Books with the University of Wales Press, later reissued by Yale University Press. The Internet Archive copy is a lending copy scanned on 9 June 2022; 2022 is the scan date, not the publication date. The book's own entry for Llandough near Penarth (pp.378–379) describes the church of St Dochdwy, the Irbic Cross and Llandough Hospital; it describes no house or farm in the parish. No entry in the book names Great House Farm, Tŷ Mawr or Cydfin.

records.title: Newman 1995, p.378: St Dochdwy, Llandough, rebuilt 1865–6 by S.C. Fripp
records.place_text: Llandough-juxta-Penarth (Llandough, 2 m. NW of Penarth), church of St Dochdwy
records.description: Newman's gazetteer entry for the parish church of Llandough near Penarth: rebuilt 1865–6 to the design of S.C. Fripp of Bristol, with a neo-Norman arch in the south aisle that replicates a 12th-century arch of the previous church.
records.transcript: ST DOCHDWY. 1865-6 by S.C. Fripp of Bristol. Elegant SE tower, an idealized version of the local type, unbuttressed under a steep saddleback roof. Tall, narrow belfry windows. The tower composes with the W front when seen from the road. Five-light W window with geometrical tracery, lean-to aisles of awkwardly shallow roof pitch. Lower chancel, barely extending beyond the tower, with lean-to N vestry. Inside, the shock is the Butterfieldian brickwork of the walls. Red, with black and white cruciform patterns in the spandrels of the nave arcades, the chancel entirely red. Circular piers of Bath stone with heavy square caps. Nave roof of local type, arch-braced with a collar purlin. At the E end of the S aisle a neo-Norman arch with much zigzag. This replicates (faithfully?) a C12 arch in the previous church.

records.title: Newman 1995, p.378: the Irbic Cross, Llandough churchyard
records.place_text: Llandough-juxta-Penarth (Llandough, 2 m. NW of Penarth), churchyard of St Dochdwy
records.description: Newman's description of the Irbic Cross in Llandough churchyard: a four-part shaft of Sutton stone, 9 ft 10 in. high, lacking only the cross-head, with the name IRBICI on the west side, decoration dated by the book to the late 10th and early 11th centuries.
records.transcript: In the CHURCHYARD stands the so-called IRBIC CROSS, the most impressive of all the visible remains of Glamorgan's Celtic Christianity, a strong reinforcement of the documentary tradition that there was a monastic establishment at Llandough in the pre-Conquest period. The cross shaft stands 9 ft 10 in. (3 metres) high and consists of four parts: a base, a lower shaft of rectangular section, a massive knop, and a square-section upper shaft, all shaped from blocks of Sutton stone. Only the cross-head itself is missing. Every surface is carved in relief. On the tapering faces of the base are busts of men (N and S), a figure on horseback (W) and a row of five standing figures, apparently ecclesiastics (E). The lower shaft has rounded angle-shafts with strong entasis, and large patterns of interlace all over. The name IRBICI appears here at the top of the W side. The knop is subdivided into five horizontal bands, each with its own interlace pattern, and forms a base for the upper shaft. This has interlace on its four faces, and plain angle rolls. Such decoration is typical of the late C10 and early C11.

records.title: Newman 1995, pp.378–379: Llandough Hospital, completed 1934
records.place_text: Llandough-juxta-Penarth (Llandough, 2 m. NW of Penarth), Llandough Hospital, ¼ m. SW of the church
records.description: Newman's entry for Llandough Hospital: by Willmott & Smith, completed 1934, with a nurses' home, additions of 1965–76 and an ante-natal clinic of 1984.
records.transcript: LLANDOUGH HOSPITAL, ¼m. SW. By Willmott & Smith, completed in 1934. Neo-Georgian, brick with stone dressings. Symmetrical plan, the ward blocks forming pavilions l. and r. of the administration block. The architects had trouble encompassing within their classicism the expanses of glass required by modern hospital wards. Five-storey NURSES' HOME by the entrance. To the S of the main building various additions, 1965-76 by the Percy Thomas Partnership (design partner Wallace Sweet). To the N, ANTE-NATAL CLINIC, 1984, by the Alex Gordon Partnership (cf. their Princess of Wales Hospital, Bridgend).

Williams, Cowbridge” belong to Llandow. The mentions of Llandough on pp.44, 46 and 508 are the village near Cowbridge. None of these passages is catalogued as Llandough-juxta-Penarth material.
